Executive function across ages: 4–5 years · 5–7 years · 7–9 years · 9–12 years · 12–25 years

Inhibitory control (response inhibition and interference control)

During the 7-9 year window, children exhibit strong improvements in inhibitory control capabilities across multiple domains, with this period marking the steepest developmental gains in several key measures. Response times in the flanker task (where a target stimulus is "flanked" by distractors) show their most rapid developmental decline (within the 7- to 12-year window) between ages 7 and 9 1. This result matches large-sample "stop-signal" data, which show that the capacity to cancel an initiated response sees the same steep trajectory of improvement 2. Antisaccade work (which measures the ability to inhibit reflexive saccades toward peripheral targets) likewise shows a rapid decline in direction errors across this window, with voluntary response suppression continuing to strengthen from late childhood into adolescence; nine-year-olds commit fewer reflexive saccades than seven-year-olds but are still well short of adult levels, suggesting this is a period of rapid but incomplete consolidation 3, 4. Error rates in inhibitory control tasks. (Figure).

Planning

Closely related to inhibitory control, this period marks a qualitative shift towards proactive control: nine-year-olds increasingly maintain task goals in advance and pre-configure responses, rather than relying primarily on reactive, late correction, and they modulate that proactive stance with context (e.g cue reliability) more flexibly than younger children 5, 6; children show clear improvements in pre-move deliberation and multi-step look-ahead in both standardized planning tasks and in naturalistic settings. Across tasks designed to measure planning abilities (e.g Tower of London, Stockings of Cambridge), children in this window invest initial thinking time before the first move and, in turn, make fewer extra moves and rule violations, an pattern that is much weaker at seven and becomes reliable (but still far from adult-like) towards the end of this window 7, 8, 9, 10. In everyday scenarios, the emergence of planning abilities manifests in children making weekend plans with friends 11, reading with an explicit goal of learning about something of interest 11, 12, and fundamental advancements in prospective memory 13 (ability to take previously-planned actions, which predicts planning abilities 14). Proactive control shows up in planning scores on a standard task. (Figure).

Working memory

By nine, working memory is not just "bigger" than at seven; it’s more controllable, precise, and strategically maintained. Capacity and fidelity both improve: visual WM holds more detailed feature information and retains it with higher precision than at age seven, with school-age gains well documented across elementary years 15. This is reflected in change-detection and delayed-reproduction work showing sharper representations and less misbinding, and in broader syntheses arguing that capacity growth during the school years is genuine rather than an encoding artifact 16, 17. At nine, children also cope better with concurrent processing: the "refreshing" of items (attention briefly switching back to revive decaying traces) becomes efficient after about age seven and continues to strengthen 18, so nine-year-olds maintain lists under distraction more successfully than seven-year-olds. Updating metrics show the same shift: on n-back, 2-back accuracy rises meaningfully from 7-9 even as 1-back nears ceiling, indicating a newly robust ability to monitor, drop, and replace items online 19. Interference control is another emergent difference: nine-year-olds are less derailed by proactive interference and show a clearer capacity to actively remove outdated contents from WM, reducing intrusion errors that are common at seven 20, 21. Verbal maintenance also becomes more "adult-like": forward and backward digit span shows rapid growth across childhood 22, and by nine children are measurably better at maintaining and manipulating sequences (including on complex/listening span tasks) than at seven; in parallel, rehearsal processes become more consistently deployed and faster, with classic work 23, 24 placing the emergence and consolidation of spontaneous verbal rehearsal within this developmental window. More sophisticated organizational memory strategies (including chunking and visual imagery that reduce memory load by forming associations) also emerge during this window 25, fundamentally changing how information is encoded. Underlying these behavioral capabilities is maturation of goal maintenance and attentional control: 7- and 9-year-olds tested on complex span tasks requiring mental arithmetic show that the ability to coordinate storage and processing improves substantially across this window 26, reflecting developing central executive function. Overall, working memory expansion during this period reflects not merely increased storage capacity, but the acquisition of active maintenance mechanisms, strategic encoding operations, and executive control over the coordination of multiple concurrent cognitive processes.

Metacognition

Metacognition (which can be broken down into monitoring (confidence/uncertainty and related self-evaluations) and control (regulatory actions conditional on those evaluations)) sees a similarly steep improvement across the 7- to 9-year window, essentially emerging as an operative control system rather than a vague feeling: children not only gauge how certain they are, they use those internal signals to regulate behavior. On paired-associate learning (remembering associations between two items, often stimulus-response) and test-taking paradigms, nine-year-olds show sharper retrospective monitoring than seven-year-olds (their confidence judgments discriminate correct from incorrect answers more reliably, and they are more willing to withdraw low-confidence responses) 27. Prospective monitoring (thinking about future performance), in contrast, develops far more slowly and remains relatively inaccurate across the 7-9 year range, with children continuing to show overconfidence in predicting future recall performance even as their retrospective judgments become well-calibrated 28; converging "metamemory" work, however, indicates that during this window children begin to monitor not only familiarity but also expected memorability 29 and the absence of memory at retrieval 30, supporting more calibrated decisions about when to restudy, to seek help, or to change an answer. A 2026 cross-sectional study tests how working-memory and inhibition demands shape monitoring in children (Figure) 38. A 17-month follow-up suggests task exposure changes how executive demands affect monitoring (Figure).

A qualitative step that is typically absent at seven but present by nine is uncertainty monitoring: when items are literally unanswerable, nine-year-olds depress confidence and differentiate "guesses" from ordinary errors, whereas seven-year-olds tend to treat difficult and unanswerable items similarly, evidence that meta-level representations of "I don’t know" have become actionable 31, 32, 33. Similarly, work on children’s understanding of inference as a source of knowledge finds that, relative to 7-year-olds, 9-year-olds become more consistent in judging knowledge gained by valid deduction as more certain than knowledge gained by perception in noisy conditions or by guessing, and they begin to explicitly justify this in terms of the structure of the argument rather than the vividness of the evidence 34. In reading, nine-year-olds engage in more effective comprehension monitoring: they allocate time to inconsistencies and better detect contradictions in text, and individual differences in this monitoring explain unique variance in comprehension beyond vocabulary and working memory 35, marking a real behavioral gain in this period; this performance-monitoring loop also shows up in arithmetic tasks, where 7- to 9-year-olds show measurable error detection and adjustment signatures (e.g., post-error slowing/accuracy improvements) that correlate with arithmetic accuracy 36. Fine-grained feedback appears to be a potent tool for encouraging accurate self-evaluations (and self-regulation) in children and adults 37.

Conclusion

Collectively, 7- to 9-year gains in executive function cohere into a single control stack: planning becomes viable precisely because working memory can buffer subgoals and constraints, response inhibition can suppress prepotent or distractor-driven moves, and metacognitive monitoring can track uncertainty and trigger strategy shifts midstream. By nine, executive function is still capacity-limited and not yet adult-like, but the core infrastructure for flexible, goal-directed control is operational: children maintain goals proactively, rehearse and update task-relevant information, inhibit counterproductive impulses, and use confidence signals to decide whether to proceed, pause, or seek more information. That integrated control noticeably lifts non-EF abilities: in language, better goal maintenance and error monitoring support comprehension checks and repair when texts conflict; in social cognition, improved inhibitory control and self-monitoring enable perspective-taking, turn-taking, and reputation-aware restraint; in mental rotation, stronger maintenance and interference control stabilize intermediate transforms and dampen egocentric pull; and in navigation/cognitive mapping, proactive planning plus flexible set-shifting supports route planning, detours, and switching between landmark-based and survey-like strategies.

Bring it all together
